mechanisms.name: Ackermann steering linkage
mechanisms.summary: A trapezoid of axle, steering arms and tie rod that turns the inner front wheel more than the outer so both roll round one centre.

ratio.typical: outer angle about 0.83 x inner angle at 30° (24.9° vs 30°)

topology.notes: four-bar: axle beam (ground), left knuckle arm, tie rod, right knuckle arm; real cars add a rack or drag link to drive it

explain.motion: Each front wheel steers about its kingpin on a knuckle with a steering arm. The arms point inward toward the centre of the rear axle and are joined by a tie rod, forming a trapezoid. When one wheel steers, the tie rod turns the other wheel by a smaller angle on the outside of the turn.
explain.forces: Steering force enters one knuckle and crosses to the other through the tie rod in push or pull. Tyre side forces feed back through the same path, so the linkage is fully backdrivable.
explain.benefits: Wheels roll on concentric circles at low speed, cutting tyre scrub and wear and making tight turns smooth.
explain.limits: A four-bar only approximates the ideal relation, best near one design angle. At high speed tyre slip angles matter more, so race cars often use parallel or reverse Ackermann.

mechanisms.name: Bell crank
mechanisms.summary: A two-armed lever on one pivot that turns a push or pull through an angle, usually 90°, and can change its size by the arm ratio.

ratio.typical: force ratio = input arm / output arm, typically 1:3 to 3:1

topology.notes: modelled as ground, bell crank, input rod and output rod with the output on a guide (6 links, 5 revolute, 2 prismatic if both rods end in sliders)

explain.motion: The L-shaped lever turns about its corner pivot. A rod pulling on one arm swings it, and the other arm, set at about 90°, pushes or pulls a second rod in a new direction. For small swings the output motion is the input motion times the arm ratio.
explain.forces: Moments balance about the pivot, so output force = input force x input arm / output arm. The pivot carries the vector sum of both rod forces; rod angles away from 90° to the arms reduce effectiveness.
explain.benefits: Redirects force around corners in a compact, stiff, easily adjusted package. Arm ratio sets the gain without gears.
explain.limits: Output is only linear with input for small swings; large angles add cosine error. Pins and rod ends wear and add play.

mechanisms.name: Eccentric sheave and strap
mechanisms.summary: An off-centre disc on a shaft, ringed by a strap and rod, works as a crank with no break in the shaft to drive a valve or pump.

ratio.typical: travel = 2 x eccentricity (24 mm with e = 12 mm)

topology.notes: sheave (crank of radius e), strap and rod, valve rod slider, ground; the large sheave-in-strap bearing is the crank pin; count includes ground

explain.motion: A round disc is keyed to the shaft with its centre offset by the eccentricity e. A strap rides round the disc and its rod pushes a slider, so the disc acts like a crank of radius e. Because the shaft passes straight through, the eccentric can sit anywhere along a crankshaft.
explain.forces: The rod force acts through the large sheave bearing, which has big rubbing area and friction. That makes the eccentric good for light loads like valves and poor for driving heavy power strokes; it is rarely backdriven.
explain.benefits: Gives a small crank throw anywhere on a continuous shaft without a split crank. Setting the sheave angle (angular advance) times the valve directly.
explain.limits: Large diameter bearing means high friction and heat, and the throw is small. Motion is only near-harmonic because the rod tilts.

mechanisms.name: Four-bar linkage
mechanisms.summary: A crank turns fully while a rocker swings back and forth, and every point on the coupler between them traces a closed curve.

ratio.typical: rocker swing 73.8° per crank turn; time ratio about 1.36 with default lengths

topology.notes: crank, coupler, rocker and ground; count includes ground

explain.motion: The short crank turns continuously about O2. The coupler carries that motion to the rocker, which can only swing back and forth over a fixed arc about O4. Every point on the coupler traces its own closed coupler curve, and choosing that point is how designers make the linkage draw a path.
explain.forces: With no load on the coupler it is a two-force member, pushing or pulling only along the line between its pins. How well that push turns the rocker depends on the transmission angle at B, best near 90° and poor below about 40°.
explain.benefits: Only four pin joints and no sliding surfaces, so it is cheap, stiff and long-lived. Changing four lengths gives an enormous range of output motions and coupler paths.
explain.limits: Output motion is fixed by the geometry and is never exact for a given function, only approximate. Near the extreme rocker positions the transmission angle falls and the linkage can bind or chatter if backdriven.

mechanisms.name: Pantograph
mechanisms.summary: A jointed parallelogram that copies any path traced by a stylus, scaled up or down by a fixed ratio.

ratio.typical: scale = OE / OT, 2:1 here; drawing pantographs typically 1:1 to 10:1

topology.notes: two long arms and two short bars forming a parallelogram, plus ground; pivot, elbow, two midpoints, stylus and pen joints; count includes ground

explain.motion: Two long arms hinge at the elbow A, and two short bars complete a parallelogram between their midpoints and the stylus T. However the stylus moves, the fixed pivot O, the stylus and the pen E stay on one straight line with the pen twice as far from O. So the pen copies every path of the stylus at twice the size.
explain.forces: Drawing loads are tiny; the bars mainly carry push and pull. Friction at the pen and the weight of long arms, plus play in the pins, scale up with the ratio and blur fine detail.
explain.benefits: Exact geometric scaling of any path with only pin joints, adjustable by moving pivots along the bars. Works in reverse to reduce.
explain.limits: Errors and pin play are magnified by the scale ratio. Reach is limited near full stretch where the elbow straightens.

mechanisms.name: Parallelogram linkage
mechanisms.summary: Opposite links of equal length keep the coupler always parallel to the frame, so it translates without turning.

ratio.typical: output crank turns exactly with the input, 1:1

topology.notes: two equal cranks, coupler equal to the frame; count includes ground

explain.motion: The two cranks are equal and the coupler equals the frame, so the four pins always form a parallelogram. Both cranks turn together at the same speed and the coupler moves in a circular translation, staying parallel to the frame while every point on it circles at crank radius.
explain.forces: Load on the coupler is shared by both cranks with no twisting of the coupler. When both cranks line up with the frame the linkage reaches a change point where it can flip into an antiparallelogram, so a third crank or a guide is needed to pass it under load.
explain.benefits: Exact 1:1 transfer and pure translation of the coupler with only pin joints. Easy to stack for lamps, lifts and tool holders.
explain.limits: At the two change points the motion is indeterminate and the linkage can switch branches. Needs a third offset crank or stiff guide to be driven reliably through full rotation.

mechanisms.name: Scissor lift
mechanisms.summary: Stacked pairs of crossed bars extend vertically when their bottom ends are pushed together, raising a platform that stays level.

ratio.typical: lift per unit slider travel = n w / h, here from about 0.6 (raised) to 8.6 (lowered)

topology.notes: 3 stages: 6 bars, ground, bottom carriage and platform, plus slot block; middle and end pins counted separately; a pin-in-slot at the top platform; count includes ground

explain.motion: Each stage is a pair of equal bars pinned at their middles like scissors, and the stages are pinned end to end. One bottom bar end is fixed and the other rides on a slider. Pushing that slider toward the fixed pin narrows every stage and each gets taller, so the platform rises by the sum of all the stage gains while staying level.
explain.forces: Platform load W needs a horizontal slider force F = W n w / h, so the push is huge when the lift is nearly flat and small when it is high. Bars carry bending as well as axial load; the lowest position is where actuators work hardest.
explain.benefits: Very compact when lowered and tall when raised, with a level platform and simple pin joints. Stages can be added for more height.
explain.limits: Force demand at the bottom of travel is very high, and stiffness falls with height so tall lifts sway. Pin wear multiplies through all stages.

mechanisms.name: Scotch yoke
mechanisms.summary: A crank pin sliding in a slotted yoke drives a rod back and forth in exact simple harmonic motion.

ratio.typical: stroke = 2 x crank radius (80 mm with r = 40 mm)

topology.notes: crank, yoke and ground; crank pin in yoke slot is a pin-in-slot higher pair (a sliding block makes it 4 links, 2 revolute, 2 prismatic)

explain.motion: The crank pin runs up and down in the yoke slot while its sideways movement carries the yoke with it. The yoke position is exactly the crank radius times the cosine of the crank angle, so the output is pure simple harmonic motion with no connecting rod to tilt.
explain.forces: The pin pushes on the slot wall at right angles to the slot, and only the component along the guide moves the yoke. Torque transfer is greatest mid-stroke and zero at the ends; contact stress at the pin and slot is high, so wear concentrates there.
explain.benefits: Exact sinusoidal output, shorter than a slider-crank for the same stroke and with no rod angle side thrust. In valve actuators run in reverse it gives high torque at the start and end of a quarter turn.
explain.limits: The sliding pin-in-slot contact wears and needs lubrication or a roller block. Not suited to high speeds with heavy loads, and in actuators it is poor for fine positioning.

mechanisms.name: Slider-crank
mechanisms.summary: A turning crank and a connecting rod drive a slider straight back and forth, the heart of every piston engine and pump.

ratio.typical: stroke = 2 x crank radius (70 mm with r = 35 mm)

topology.notes: crank, connecting rod, slider and ground; count includes ground

explain.motion: The crank turns at constant speed and the slider runs back and forth along its guide with a stroke of twice the crank radius. Because the rod is tilted for most of the turn, the slider motion is not a pure sine: it moves faster in the half of the stroke nearer the crank. Run backwards, a pushed slider turns the crank, as in an engine.
explain.forces: The rod is a two-force member and carries only push or pull. Its tilt (obliquity) splits that force into a useful axial part and a side thrust on the guide walls. At the two dead centres the rod lines up with the crank and a slider force produces no torque at all.
explain.benefits: Simple, compact and able to carry very large loads with plain bearings. Turns rotation into straight reciprocation, or the reverse, with a fixed stroke.
explain.limits: A slider-driven crank cannot start from a dead centre and needs a flywheel or a second cylinder to carry it through. Side thrust wears the guide, and the motion carries second-harmonic shaking forces.

mechanisms.name: Trammel of Archimedes
mechanisms.summary: Two blocks sliding in crossed grooves carry a rod whose points draw exact ellipses.

ratio.typical: ellipse half-axes = distances from pen to each block (40 x 100 mm here)

topology.notes: ground with crossed grooves, two blocks, rod, and a drive crank to the rod midpoint (redundant constraint); count includes ground

explain.motion: One block slides along the horizontal groove and the other along the vertical one, and a rod joins them. A crank from the crossing to the rod midpoint turns it round. The blocks pass through the crossing one at a time, and a pen on the extended rod traces an ellipse whose half-axes are its distances to the two blocks.
explain.forces: Each groove can only push its block at right angles to the groove, so the blocks feel side forces only. Driving from the midpoint crank works but the crank and rod rotate in opposite directions, causing friction and wear at the midpoint pin.
explain.benefits: Exact ellipses of any proportion from two adjustable distances on a straight bar, with no curved guide. The blocks themselves give exact straight-line motion and the midpoint traces a circle.
explain.limits: Sliders need clean, low-play grooves or the ellipse distorts. Blocks must pass through the crossing, so the groove ends need cut-backs.

mechanisms.name: Antiparallelogram linkage
mechanisms.summary: A crossed four-bar with opposite links equal: the two cranks turn in opposite directions at varying speeds, like a pair of elliptical gears.

ratio.typical: 1:1 average, reversed; instantaneous 0.43x to 2.33x with defaults

topology.notes: two long crossed cranks, short coupler equal to the short frame; count includes ground

explain.motion: The two long links cross like scissors. With the short link fixed, both long cranks make full turns in opposite directions, and their crossing point stays on an ellipse whose foci are the fixed pivots, exactly like a pair of rolling elliptical gears. The midpoint of the free long link traces a figure-eight.
explain.forces: Each crank drives the other through the short coupler as push or pull. The speed ratio and torque ratio change continuously and are inverses of each other, so torque rises when the output slows.
explain.benefits: An exact, gearless replacement for elliptical gears and a compact way to reverse rotation with a built-in speed variation. A building block for Kempe angle multipliers and Hart's inversor.
explain.limits: Passes through change points where it can flip into a parallelogram, so it needs bracing or a guide. Large speed variation causes heavy inertia loads at speed.

mechanisms.name: Centrifugal governor
mechanisms.summary: Spinning weights swing out as speed rises and lift a sleeve that can close a throttle, holding an engine near a set speed.

ratio.typical: ball height below pivot h = g / omega^2 (Watt type)

topology.notes: frame, spindle, 2 ball arms, 2 links, sleeve; sleeve slides on the spindle; dof 2 = spindle speed plus ball height, the height settled by dynamics

explain.motion: Two balls on arms hinged at the top of a vertical spindle are swung round by the engine. As speed rises they fly outward and upward like a conical pendulum, and links from the arms pull a sleeve up the spindle. The sleeve moves a lever that closes the steam valve or opens it again when speed falls.
explain.forces: Centrifugal force on each ball, m omega^2 times its radius, balances gravity and the sleeve load through the arm angle. The sleeve can supply only a small force, and friction in the sleeve and valve linkage makes the governor insensitive to small speed changes.
explain.benefits: Automatic feedback speed control with no external power, simple and robust, and a classic visual of control engineering.
explain.limits: The plain Watt governor has small sleeve force and changes speed setting with load (proportional droop), and can hunt or oscillate. Not usable at high speeds without springs or dead weights (Porter, Hartnell types).

mechanisms.name: Double-crank linkage
mechanisms.summary: A four-bar with the shortest link fixed, so both side links turn full circles but the output speeds up and slows down each turn.

ratio.typical: 1:1 average; output speed swings 0.51x to 2.07x input with defaults

topology.notes: input crank, coupler, output crank and short ground link; count includes ground

explain.motion: With the shortest link as the frame, both links pinned to it can make full turns. The input crank turns steadily and the output crank also goes round once per turn, but it lags and leads, so its speed varies through the cycle.
explain.forces: Torque passes through the coupler as push or pull. The transmission angle stays reasonable (24° to 78° with defaults) as long as the frame is much shorter than the others, but it is lowest when the cranks are nearly aligned with the frame.
explain.benefits: Gives a continuous rotary output with built-in speed variation, useful for quick-return drives and for feeding a slider-crank. Only pin joints.
explain.limits: The very short frame link makes the two bearings crowded and the cranks overlap. Speed variation is fixed by the geometry and cannot be adjusted in use.

mechanisms.name: Double-rocker linkage
mechanisms.summary: A four-bar in which neither ground-pivoted link can turn fully: an input lever swings and drives an output lever through a different arc.

ratio.typical: input swing about 70° gives output swing about 41° with defaults

topology.notes: two rockers, coupler and ground; count includes ground

explain.motion: Both links pinned to the frame can only swing over limited arcs. When the coupler is the shortest link, it can turn fully relative to the rockers, but the rockers themselves stop at toggle positions where the coupler lines up with one of them.
explain.forces: The coupler carries push or pull only. At each end of the input range the coupler is in line with the output rocker, the transmission angle approaches 0° or 180°, and the linkage cannot be driven further from the input.
explain.benefits: Converts one swing into another with a chosen, non-linear relation, and can be designed to hold a load near a toggle. Common for steering and luffing where neither side needs to rotate fully.
explain.limits: Range is bounded by toggle positions where the linkage locks or jumps branch. Transmission angle varies a lot, so drive torque must rise near the ends.

mechanisms.name: Five-bar linkage
mechanisms.summary: A closed loop of five bars with two driven cranks, so one end point can be steered anywhere in a planar workspace.

ratio.typical: 2 inputs map to an x-y point; scale set by arm lengths

topology.notes: two grounded motors; a gear pair between the cranks makes it a 1-DOF geared five-bar

explain.motion: Two cranks turn about fixed pivots O1 and O2. Each carries a distal bar, and the two distal bars meet at the tip P. Setting both crank angles fixes P, so moving them together steers P along any path in the workspace.
explain.forces: Both motors sit on the base, so the moving parts are light and forces at P are shared by two arms. Near singular poses (distal bars in line, or a crank in line with its distal bar) stiffness or control is lost.
explain.benefits: Low moving inertia, high stiffness and easy backdriving make it good for fast pick-and-place, plotters and haptic devices.
explain.limits: The workspace is smaller than a serial arm's and is bounded by singularities. Two motors and inverse kinematics are needed.

mechanisms.name: Oscillating cylinder engine
mechanisms.summary: A cylinder rocks on a trunnion while its piston rod drives a crank directly, so the swing of the cylinder also opens and closes its ports.

ratio.typical: stroke = 2 x crank radius (70 mm); cylinder swing ±asin(r/d) = ±17°

topology.notes: crank, piston and rod, cylinder and ground; the swinging-block inversion of the slider-crank; count includes ground

explain.motion: The piston rod is pinned straight to the crank pin and the cylinder hangs on a trunnion so it can rock to follow the rod. As the crank turns, the piston slides in and out of the bore while the whole cylinder swings a few degrees either side. Holes in the swinging port face line up with steam and exhaust holes in the fixed standard, so the swing itself does the valve timing.
explain.forces: Steam pressure on the piston pushes along the cylinder axis straight into the crank pin, and the trunnion takes the reaction. Torque is zero at the two dead centres, so a flywheel carries it through; a spring holds the port faces together and limits pressure.
explain.benefits: Very few parts: no crosshead, no connecting rod and no separate valve gear. Easy to make, self-starting in most positions with a double-acting or twin layout.
explain.limits: The sliding port face leaks and wears, and the spring-loaded face limits steam pressure. Large cylinders have heavy swinging masses.

mechanisms.name: Stephenson six-bar linkage
mechanisms.summary: A four-bar whose coupler point drives an extra two-link dyad, so the output follows the coupler curve and can dwell or swing widely.

ratio.typical: about 54° of output swing per crank turn here

topology.notes: Stephenson topology: ternary ground and ternary coupler separated by binary links; one four-bar loop and one five-bar loop

explain.motion: A crank-rocker four-bar O2-A-B-O4 has a triangular coupler; a point P on it traces a closed coupler curve. A link P-D ties that point to an output rocker O6-D, so the rocker follows the curve. Where the curve runs along an arc centred on D, the output pauses.
explain.forces: Crank torque passes through the ternary coupler and the dyad link, each pin-ended bar carrying push or pull. The output rocker sees high force but little motion near its toggle positions.
explain.benefits: It can give dwells, large swings or special timing with only pin joints and one input.
explain.limits: Coupler curves are sensitive to dimensions and wear, and branch flips are possible if the dyad nears a straight line. Design needs simulation or synthesis software.

mechanisms.name: Toggle clamp
mechanisms.summary: A handle drives a link nearly into line with its arm, multiplying hand force hugely and locking just past centre.

ratio.typical: mechanical advantage rises without limit toward toggle; about 10:1 to 60:1 in the last few degrees

topology.notes: handle, link, plunger and ground: a slider-crank used near dead centre; count includes ground

explain.motion: Pushing the handle swings its short arm round the pivot and the link drives the plunger out along its guides. Near the end of the throw the arm and link come into line, the toggle position, and the plunger almost stops while the handle still turns. The handle goes a few degrees past that line and rests against a stop.
explain.forces: Because the plunger barely moves for a large handle motion near toggle, the force ratio becomes very large. Just past centre a push on the plunger tries to turn the handle further onto its stop, so clamp force locks itself and the handle needs no holding.
explain.benefits: Very high clamping force from a small hand force, a positive lock, and fast open and close. Simple pin-jointed parts.
explain.limits: Clamp force depends on the exact stack height and spring of the parts, so it needs adjustment. Wear in the pins lets the lock slip, and the force is very sensitive near toggle.

mechanisms.summary: Two four-bar loops sharing a ternary rocker: a turning crank drives a first rocker, which drives a second rocker with a reshaped swing.

topology.notes: Watt topology: the two ternary links (ground and the middle rocker) share joint O4; two four-bar loops

explain.motion: A crank-rocker loop O2-A-B-O4 turns the crank's rotation into a rocking of the middle link. That middle rocker is a triangle: its second arm O4-C drives a second loop C-D-O6, so the output rocker at O6 swings by an amount and with a timing that the second loop reshapes.
explain.forces: Torque passes from the crank through two pin-ended couplers in series, so each coupler only pushes or pulls. Transmission angles in both loops must stay roughly between 40° and 140°; near a toggle in either loop the output force grows while the motion stalls.
explain.benefits: It gives more design freedom than a four-bar (amplified swing, dwell, better timing) while still using only pin joints.
explain.limits: Errors and clearances in two loops add up, and a poor second loop can lock or flip branch. Synthesis is harder than for a single four-bar.

mechanisms.name: Jansen's linkage
mechanisms.summary: Theo Jansen's Strandbeest leg: one crank and eleven bars move the foot along a long flat stride and lift it on the way back.

ratio.typical: flat stride about 4 x crank radius (124 mm at a 30 mm crank), lift about 45 mm

topology.notes: ground, crank, bars j, k, c, f, upper triangle and foot triangle; joints at A, Y and C each join three bodies

explain.motion: The crank turns about O. Bars j and k carry its motion to the upper triangle (pivoted at the fixed point Y) and to bar c, and the two rigid triangles pass it down to the foot. For about half the turn the foot slides along a nearly flat line, then it lifts and swings forward to start the next step.
explain.forces: During the stride the ground pushes up on the foot; the load travels through the foot triangle and bars into the fixed pivot Y and the crank. Every bar other than the two triangles is pinned at both ends, so it only pushes or pulls. Because the foot stays level, the crank does little lifting work during the stride.
explain.benefits: All joints are plain pins and the leg has one degree of freedom, so one shaft drives many legs. The flat stride keeps the body at a steady height.
explain.limits: Eleven bars and many pins add friction and play, and the foot path is fixed by the holy numbers. It walks well only on fairly flat ground and is slow to climb.

mechanisms.name: Klann linkage
mechanisms.summary: Joe Klann's six-bar walking leg: one crank moves a foot along a flat stance stroke and then lifts it high for the return step.

ratio.typical: foot stride about 3.8 x crank radius, lift about 2 x crank radius

topology.notes: modified Stephenson III chain; ternary connecting member and ternary leg

explain.motion: The crank turns the connecting member, whose middle pin E is held by a short lower rocker, so its far end K swings in a loop. The leg is a rigid bar pinned at the hip H to an upper rocker and at the knee K to the connecting member. The foot at its tip moves along a nearly flat line for about a third of the turn and then lifts and swings back.
explain.forces: Ground reaction at the foot travels up the leg into the two rockers and the crank, so the long leg bar sees bending. Two legs half a cycle apart on one crank share the load and keep the frame level.
explain.benefits: High foot lift lets it step over obstacles and climb stairs, using only pin joints and one rotary drive per side.
explain.limits: The stance is not perfectly flat or constant speed, and the foot path is fixed by the geometry. The long leg bar must be stiff; joint play shows up as foot wobble.

mechanisms.name: Rhombic drive
mechanisms.summary: Two geared counter-rotating cranks and a jointed rhombus drive two coaxial pistons with a phase lag and no side thrust.

ratio.typical: each piston stroke about 2.4 x crank radius here (47.7 mm at r = 20)

topology.notes: ground, two crank gears, four equal rods, power piston and displacer; the count is over-constrained and moves thanks to symmetry, the gear mesh keeps the cranks mirrored

explain.motion: Two equal gears mesh and turn in opposite directions, each with a crank pin. Four equal rods join the two pins to an upper yoke on the power piston and a lower yoke on the displacer, forming a rhombus. As the cranks turn, the rhombus flattens and stretches, and the two pistons slide along the same axis with a phase lag of about 70° to 90°.
explain.forces: Gas force on each piston splits equally into two rods, and the sideways components cancel, so the pistons need almost no side guidance. The gears carry the torque difference between the two cranks.
explain.benefits: Perfect dynamic balance with no side thrust on the seals lets beta Stirling engines run smooth, quiet and pressurised.
explain.limits: Many precise parts, close tolerances and a gear pair make it costly. Wear in the gears lets the cranks drift from mirror symmetry.

mechanisms.name: Walschaerts valve gear
mechanisms.summary: A steam locomotive linkage that mixes motion from a return crank and the crosshead to time the valve, with reversing and cutoff control.

ratio.typical: valve travel set by die position, about 2 x lap + lead in mid gear up to full travel at full gear

topology.notes: frame, wheel with crank and return crank, main rod, crosshead, eccentric rod, expansion link, radius rod, combination lever, union link, valve spindle, lifting link; die block in curved link slot counted as one higher pair; reverser setting held fixed

explain.motion: A return crank on the driving wheel, set about 90° from the main crank, drives an eccentric rod that rocks the curved expansion link about its trunnion. A die block in the link moves the radius rod, whose end drives the top of the combination lever; the bottom of that lever is driven from the crosshead through the union link. The valve spindle, pinned between them, gets the sum: a lap and lead motion from the crosshead and a variable motion from the link.
explain.forces: Valve friction and steam pressure on the valve flow back through the combination lever into the crosshead and return crank, loads that are small compared with the piston loads. The die block and link slot carry the reversing load and wear most.
explain.benefits: Mounted outside the frames for easy inspection, light, and gives constant lead at all cutoffs, with reversing and cutoff from a single reverser.
explain.limits: Geometry is approximate, so valve events are unequal front and back unless carefully proportioned. Many pins wear and add lost motion.

mechanisms.name: Chebyshev linkage
mechanisms.summary: Crossed rockers in the ratio 4:5:2 make the coupler midpoint run very nearly straight between the two pivots' verticals.

ratio.typical: stroke = ground length (120 mm here) for 53° of rocker swing

topology.notes: crossed double-rocker four-bar; tracer at coupler midpoint

explain.motion: Two long rockers pivot on a common base and cross each other; a short coupler joins their tips. When the left rocker swings from about 37° to 90°, the coupler midpoint moves from directly above one pivot to directly above the other along a nearly flat line.
explain.forces: The rockers are two-force members carrying push or pull. Near the ends of the stroke the transmission angle falls and the input torque needed rises.
explain.benefits: Very good straightness (0.3 mm over 120 mm here) from three moving pin-jointed parts.
explain.limits: Only a limited swing is straight, and the crossed rockers must sit in different planes so they can pass each other.

mechanisms.name: Roberts linkage
mechanisms.summary: Equal rockers carrying an isosceles triangle: the triangle's apex moves almost straight along the line through the two pivots.

ratio.typical: about 80 mm of near-straight travel for 34° of rocker swing (ground 100)

topology.notes: symmetric double-rocker four-bar; tracer at the apex of the triangular coupler

explain.motion: Two equal rockers stand on pivots a distance 2b apart. Their tips carry the base of a triangular coupler whose two equal sides hang down to an apex P. As the rockers lean, P slides along the ground line between the pivots, almost straight.
explain.forces: The rockers carry push or pull only; loads at P bend the coupler plate. Straightness and stiffness fall near the stroke ends where the rockers get steep.
explain.benefits: Symmetric, compact and all pin-jointed, with the straight path lying conveniently on the line of the fixed pivots.
explain.limits: Straightness is approximate and the usable stroke is shorter than the pivot spacing. The apex passes between the pivots, which constrains the frame layout.

mechanisms.name: Scott Russell linkage
mechanisms.summary: A beam pinned at its midpoint to a crank of half its length: sliding one end along a line moves the other exactly at right angles.

ratio.typical: output y = 2a sin(phi), input x = 2a cos(phi); 1:1 at 45°

topology.notes: ground, crank, beam, slider; exact straight line for the beam end

explain.motion: A crank of length a pivots at O and holds the middle M of a beam of length 2a. One end B slides along the x axis. Because O, B and P all lie on a circle centred at M of radius a, the other end P moves exactly along the y axis through O.
explain.forces: The slider guide takes side load, which rises steeply as B approaches O and the crank lines up with the beam. The crank pin at M carries the main load in push or pull.
explain.benefits: An exact straight line at right angles to the input from only one slide and three pins, more compact than a Watt's linkage.
explain.limits: It needs a sliding or rolling guide for B, and it cannot pass through the position where B reaches O. Lateral force on the slider grows near that end.

explain.motion: Two equal rockers pivot on opposite sides, one high and one low, and a short coupler joins their tips. As the rockers swing, each tip moves on an arc, and the arcs bend opposite ways, so the coupler midpoint moves almost straight. Over the full swing the midpoint draws a figure eight.
explain.forces: Each rocker is pinned at both ends, so it only pushes or pulls along its length. Loads across the line of motion are carried, which is why it locates an axle sideways.
explain.benefits: Three moving pin-jointed parts give good straight motion without sliders, and it is symmetric left to right.
explain.limits: Straightness holds only near the middle of the swing; deviation grows quickly toward the toggles. It needs room for two long rockers.

mechanisms.name: Evans grasshopper linkage
mechanisms.summary: A Scott Russell linkage with the slider replaced by a long swinging link: the beam end moves nearly straight with only pin joints.

ratio.typical: about 50 mm of near-straight travel for a 40° swing of the radius link (a = 50)

topology.notes: four-bar: radius link, beam and long swing link; tracer at the free end of the beam

explain.motion: A radius link of length a pivots at O1 and holds the middle of a beam of length 2a. One beam end B is held by a long swing link instead of a slider, so B moves on a gentle arc that is close to a straight line. The other end P then moves nearly straight along a line through O1, at right angles to B's path.
explain.forces: Load at P is shared by the radius link at mid-beam and the swing link at B; all three are pin-ended. The beam bends between its pins, and the swing link carries little load.
explain.benefits: Gives Scott Russell type straight motion without any sliding guide, so it lasts with little lubrication.

mechanisms.name: Hoekens linkage
mechanisms.summary: A crank-rocker whose extended coupler tip runs along a straight line at nearly constant speed for half of every crank turn.

ratio.typical: straight stroke = 4 x crank (160 mm at a 40 mm crank) per half turn

topology.notes: crank-rocker four-bar with the coupler extended past the rocker pin

explain.motion: A short crank turns fully about O2 and a rocker of 2.5 crank lengths swings about O4. The coupler is pinned to both and extends to a tip twice the rocker-pin distance from the crank pin. For half the crank turn the tip moves along a straight line at almost constant speed, then it returns along a raised arc.
explain.forces: The rocker is a two-force member. The long coupler overhang sees bending from any load at the tip, and the transmission angle at B should be watched near the return.
explain.benefits: Continuous crank input with a long, steady-speed straight stroke makes it a good walking leg or film-advance claw.

mechanisms.name: Tusi couple
mechanisms.summary: A gear rolling inside a ring twice its size: every point on its pitch circle moves in a perfectly straight line.

ratio.typical: stroke = ring pitch diameter = 4 x planet pitch radius (128 mm here)

topology.notes: ground with fixed 32T ring, carrier arm, 16T planet; one internal gear mesh

explain.motion: The arm carries the small gear around inside the fixed ring. Because the ring has exactly twice as many teeth, the small gear spins backwards once for each orbit, and any point on its pitch circle slides back and forth along a diameter of the ring. The two tracers here move on two straight lines at right angles.
explain.forces: Driving torque on the arm becomes a tangential tooth force against the ring, which turns the small gear. A load on the traced point acts through the gear's own pin and teeth, so there is no sliding guide at all, only rolling contact. Near the ends of the stroke the arm has little leverage on the tracer, so it cannot be driven from the tracer there.
explain.benefits: An exact straight line, and exact simple harmonic motion along it, from purely rotating parts.
explain.limits: Needs an accurate internal gear pair with exactly 2:1 teeth, and backlash shows up directly as error in the line. Points inside the pitch circle trace ellipses, not lines, so the tracer must sit exactly on the pitch circle.

Points at radius rho < r trace ellipses with semi-axes r + rho and r - rho.

mechanisms.name: Hart's inversor
mechanisms.summary: A six-bar inversor built on a crossed antiparallelogram: a point on a circle through the fixed pivot drives another along an exact line.

ratio.typical: about 113 mm of exact straight travel for ±80° of crank swing

topology.notes: ground, crank, and the four bars of an antiparallelogram (one short bar pivoted to ground at its midpoint)

explain.motion: Four bars form a crossed antiparallelogram: two long bars CD and EF and two short bars CE and FD. The midpoints of all four bars always lie on one line, and the product of distances from one midpoint to two others stays constant. With the midpoint A of CE fixed and the midpoint g of EF driven on a circle through A, the midpoint p of CD runs on an exact straight line.
explain.forces: All bars are pin-ended; the long bars also carry the mid-span pins g and p, so they see some bending. Near the ends of travel the crossed bars line up and force transmission drops.
explain.benefits: An exact straight line with six links instead of Peaucellier's eight.
explain.limits: The crank can only swing, not rotate, and the crossed bars must sit in different planes. Pins at mid-bar need stiff bars.

mechanisms.name: Peaucellier-Lipkin linkage
mechanisms.summary: An eight-bar inversor: as the input point moves on a circle through the fixed pivot, the output point moves on an exactly straight line.

ratio.typical: 175 mm of exact straight travel for ±64° of input swing

topology.notes: ground, input arm, two long arms, four rhombus sides; joints at O, A, B and C each join three bodies

explain.motion: Two long arms from the fixed pivot O hold opposite corners A and B of a rhombus whose other corners are C and D. O, C and D stay in line and OC x OD stays constant, so D is the inverse of C. A short input arm pivoted at Q makes C move on a circle through O, and the inverse of such a circle is a straight line, which D traces exactly.
explain.forces: All bars are pin-ended and carry only push or pull. Force at D reaches the input through the rhombus and long arms; mechanical advantage falls as C approaches O and D runs far out.
explain.benefits: It was the first planar linkage to give an exact straight line using only pin joints, with no slide.
explain.limits: Eight links and ten pins add play, and the arms must cross in several planes. Straight travel is limited by the arms reaching full stretch.

build.input: input arm oscillating ±64° about Q
build.output: rhombus corner D moving along x = 140
build.defining_relations: OC x OD = l^2 - q^2 = 12600 mm^2. C on a circle of radius r through O gives D on the line x = (l^2 - q^2)/(2r) = 140.

mechanisms.name: Offset slider-crank
mechanisms.summary: A slider-crank whose slide line misses the crank centre, so the forward and return strokes take different crank angles.

ratio.typical: stroke slightly over 2r (61.4 mm for r = 30); time ratio 1.09:1 for e = 20

topology.notes: ground, crank, connecting rod, slider

explain.motion: The crank turns at constant speed and the rod pushes a slider along a line that is offset from the crank centre by e. The slider's two dead centres occur where crank and rod are in line, and because of the offset these two crank positions are not 180° apart. One stroke therefore takes slightly more crank angle than the other.
explain.forces: The rod force splits into a useful push along the slide and a side thrust on the guide; offsetting the crank reduces rod angularity during the working stroke, which lowers side thrust and friction there. Near the dead centres the crank has no leverage on the slider.
explain.benefits: The simplest quick-return, with only one more parameter than an ordinary slider-crank, and offset engines (desaxe) gain lower piston side load.
explain.limits: Only small time ratios are practical, as large offsets give poor transmission angles and high side thrust on the return stroke.

mechanisms.name: Crank and slotted lever quick-return
mechanisms.summary: A crank pin slides in a slotted lever that rocks about a pivot below, pushing a ram slowly forward to cut and pulling it back fast.

ratio.typical: cut:return = (180° + 2 asin(r/d)) : (180° - 2 asin(r/d)), 1.71:1 here; stroke 128 mm

topology.notes: ground, crank, slide block, slotted lever, link, ram; block slides in the lever slot (prismatic), ram on rails (prismatic)

explain.motion: The crank turns at constant speed and its pin, in a sliding block, drives a slotted lever that rocks about a pivot below the crank. The lever swings through the same angle either way, but the crank takes the long way round the circle for the cutting stroke and the short way for the return. A short link at the top of the lever pushes the ram along its rails.
explain.forces: The crank pin pushes the block at right angles to the slot, so the lever sees a torque that is largest when the pin is farthest from the lever pivot, which is during the cut. The cutting load on the ram returns through the link, lever pivot and block; side thrust on the ram goes into the rails.
explain.benefits: Simple, robust and gives a slow, nearly uniform cutting stroke with a quick idle return, saving cycle time.
explain.limits: Ram speed is not constant during the cut, and the block and slot wear and need lubrication. The time ratio is fixed by r/d; changing stroke by changing r also changes the ratio.

mechanisms.name: Whitworth quick-return
mechanisms.summary: A crank pin drives a slotted lever that turns fully round an offset pivot, so a rod-driven ram cuts slowly and returns quickly.

ratio.typical: cut:return = (180° + 2 asin(e/r)) : (180° - 2 asin(e/r)), 1.59:1 here; stroke = 2R = 64 mm

topology.notes: ground, 16T pinion, 50T bull gear (crank), slide block, slotted lever, rod, ram; one gear mesh

explain.motion: A pinion drives the bull gear, whose crank pin carries a block sliding in a slotted lever. The lever pivot sits inside the crank circle, offset by e, so the lever turns a full revolution but at varying speed. A short arm on the far side of the lever drives a connecting rod and ram, which moves slowly while the lever turns the long way and quickly on the short way.
explain.forces: Torque flows from pinion to bull gear, then as a normal force from the pin block onto the slot walls, then through the lever arm R and rod into the ram. The lever torque from the cutting load is largest when the slot is most tilted, loading the block and offset pivot.
explain.benefits: Smoother lever motion than the oscillating slotted lever, a compact layout with a short lever, and a fixed, reliable time ratio.
explain.limits: The ram speed varies through the stroke, and the time ratio depends only on e/r so it cannot be adjusted on the fly. Slot and block wear add backlash at stroke reversals.

mechanisms.name: Drag-link quick-return
mechanisms.summary: A double-crank four-bar turns uniform input into uneven output rotation, which drives a ram slowly one way and fast back.

ratio.typical: time ratio about 1.5:1 here (216.5° : 143.5°); stroke about 2 x ram crank radius

topology.notes: ground, input crank, coupler, output crank (with ram arm), connecting rod, ram

explain.motion: The fixed link is the shortest of a Grashof four-bar, so both cranks turn fully round. When the input turns at constant speed, the output crank speeds up over one half turn and slows down over the other. An arm fixed to the output crank drives a connecting rod and ram, and the ram's slow stroke is placed where the output crank is slow.
explain.forces: Torque passes from the input crank through the coupler to the output crank; the transmission angle swings widely, so force transfer is weakest when the coupler and output crank are nearly in line. The ram load comes back through the rod onto the output crank pivot.
explain.benefits: Only pin joints, no slots or sliding blocks except the ram, so it runs quietly and wears little.
explain.limits: The fixed link is short so the pivots crowd together, and the time ratio is modest unless transmission angles become poor (minimum about 30° here).

mechanisms.name: Rack and pinion
mechanisms.summary: A gear meshing with a straight toothed bar: every turn of the pinion moves the rack one pitch-circle circumference.

ratio.typical: travel = pitch radius x angle; 100.5 mm per pinion turn at m = 4, z = 16

explain.motion: The pinion swings back and forth and the rack slides with it. The rack moves exactly the pinion's pitch radius times the angle turned, so travel is proportional to rotation in both directions.
explain.forces: Torque on the pinion becomes a straight push on the rack equal to torque divided by pitch radius. The 20° pressure angle adds a force pushing rack and pinion apart, which the rack guide or a backing roller must resist so the teeth cannot climb out.

mechanisms.name: Spur gear pair
mechanisms.summary: Two involute gears on parallel shafts turn in opposite directions at a fixed speed ratio set by their tooth counts.

ratio.typical: 1:1 to about 6:1 per pair; default 28/14 = 2:1

topology.notes: ground, pinion, gear; one gear mesh higher pair

explain.motion: The 14-tooth pinion drives the 28-tooth gear, so the gear turns half as fast and the other way. Involute teeth roll and slide against each other so that the speed ratio stays exactly constant at every instant of the mesh, not just on average.
explain.forces: Tooth contact always lies on the line of action, tilted by the 20° pressure angle from the common tangent of the pitch circles. The tangential part turns the gear while the radial part pushes the shafts apart into the bearings; halving the speed doubles the torque, less about 1 to 2% friction.
explain.benefits: Constant velocity ratio, about 98% efficiency, simple to make and inspect, and the ratio is exact because it is counted in teeth. Involute teeth tolerate small centre-distance errors without changing the ratio.
explain.limits: Teeth engage across the full face at once, so spur gears are noisier than helical gears at speed. Ratios above about 6:1 in one pair need a tiny pinion that suffers undercut (below 17 teeth at 20° without profile shift).

mechanisms.name: Bevel gear pair
mechanisms.summary: Cone-shaped gears transmit rotation between intersecting shafts, usually at a right angle, with a fixed ratio.

ratio.typical: 1:1 (mitre) to about 6:1; default 32/16 = 2:1

topology.notes: ground, pinion, gear; one bevel mesh; pitch cones share an apex at the shaft intersection

explain.motion: Two toothed cones roll on each other with a common apex where the shafts cross. The 16-tooth pinion turns the 32-tooth gear at half speed about an axis at 90°, and the pitch cone angles (26.6° and 63.4°) are set by the tooth ratio.
explain.forces: Tooth force splits into tangential, radial and axial parts; both gears are pushed away from the cone apex along their own axes, so each shaft needs a thrust-capable bearing. Load is concentrated toward the large end of the tooth.
explain.benefits: The simplest way to turn a drive through a corner with an exact ratio and high efficiency (about 97 to 98%).
explain.limits: Mounting must be precise because both apexes must coincide; errors shift the contact patch and cause noise or tooth breakage. Straight bevels are noisy at speed, so spiral bevels are used there.

mechanisms.name: Compound gear train
mechanisms.summary: Two gear pairs stacked on a shared middle shaft multiply their ratios, giving 3 x 3 = 9:1 in a compact space.

ratio.typical: product of stage ratios, e.g. 3 x 3 = 9:1; 2 stages give up to about 40:1

topology.notes: ground, input pinion a, cluster b+c (one rigid body), output gear d; two gear meshes

explain.motion: A 12-tooth input pinion drives a 36-tooth gear three times slower. A second 12-tooth pinion fixed to that same shaft, one layer up, drives a final 36-tooth gear another three times slower, so the output turns once for every nine input turns, in the same direction as the input.
explain.forces: Torque grows stage by stage: about 3x on the cluster shaft and 9x on the output, so the last mesh carries the highest tooth load and usually needs the widest face. Each mesh loses 1 to 2% to friction, so efficiency is the product of stage efficiencies.
explain.benefits: A single 9:1 pair would need a gear nine times the pinion size; compounding reaches the same ratio with small gears, and every extra stage multiplies the ratio again.
explain.limits: More stages add backlash, inertia and parts. Direction depends on the number of external meshes, and high ratios are usually more compact as planetary or worm drives.

mechanisms.name: Helical gear pair
mechanisms.summary: Gears with teeth cut on a helix engage gradually, running quieter and stronger than spur gears but pushing their shafts axially.

ratio.typical: 1:1 to about 10:1 per pair; default 34/17 = 2:1

topology.notes: ground, pinion, gear; one helical gear mesh (line contact sweeps diagonally across the face)

explain.motion: Seen end-on, a helical pair behaves exactly like a spur pair: the 17-tooth pinion drives the 34-tooth gear at half speed in the opposite direction. Along the face the teeth are twisted at 20°, so each tooth comes into contact at one end and the contact line sweeps across, with several teeth always sharing load.
explain.forces: The tooth force has a tangential part that does the work, a radial part, and an axial thrust equal to tangential force times tan(helix angle), here about 36% of it. That thrust must be taken by thrust-capable bearings, and the two gears must have opposite hands.
explain.benefits: Gradual engagement and a higher total contact ratio give much quieter running and higher load capacity than spur gears of the same size, which is why nearly all car gearboxes use them.
explain.limits: Axial thrust needs angular-contact or tapered bearings, and extra sliding lowers efficiency slightly. Gears cannot be slid in and out of mesh as easily as spur gears.

mechanisms.name: Herringbone gear pair
mechanisms.summary: Two opposite-hand helical halves side by side cancel each other's axial thrust, giving smooth, heavy-duty parallel-shaft drive.

ratio.typical: 1:1 to about 10:1 per pair; default 40/20 = 2:1

topology.notes: ground, pinion, gear; one double-helical mesh; one shaft usually allowed to float axially

explain.motion: Each gear is two helical gears of opposite hand joined face to face, forming a V of teeth. End-on it behaves like a spur pair, while along the face both halves engage gradually and many teeth share the load.
explain.forces: The axial thrust of the left half (Ft/2 x tan beta) is equal and opposite to that of the right half, so they cancel and only radial bearings are needed. One shaft is left free to float axially so the two halves share load equally.
explain.benefits: Allows large helix angles (25° to 45°) for very smooth, high-capacity drive without thrust bearings; historically key to marine steam turbine reduction gears.
explain.limits: Hard to manufacture accurately (needs a central relief groove or a Sykes-type shaper), and a mismatch between halves overloads one side. More expensive than single helical gears.

mechanisms.summary: A pinion meshes inside a ring with teeth on its inner rim, so both turn the same way on close, parallel shafts.

explain.motion: The 18-tooth pinion rolls inside a 40-tooth internal gear. Because the teeth meet on the same side of both centres, ring and pinion turn in the same direction, the ring at 18/40 of the pinion speed.
explain.forces: A concave ring tooth wraps around a convex pinion tooth, so contact stress is lower and more teeth share the load than in an external pair. The radial separating force acts toward the ring centre and is taken by both bearings.
explain.benefits: Very short centre distance (half the tooth-count difference times the module), same-direction rotation without an idler, and a natural housing for planetary sets.

mechanisms.name: Sun and planet gear
mechanisms.summary: A planet gear fixed to a beam engine's connecting rod orbits a sun gear on the flywheel shaft, turning the shaft twice per orbit.

ratio.typical: shaft turns = 1 + zp/zs per planet orbit; 2 turns per beam double stroke with equal gears

topology.notes: ground, beam, connecting rod with planet rigidly fixed, sun with flywheel, retaining link from sun shaft to planet centre; one gear mesh

explain.motion: The beam rocks and drives the connecting rod, whose lower end carries a planet gear that cannot turn relative to the rod. A retaining link keeps the planet in mesh as its centre orbits the sun gear on the flywheel shaft. Because the planet does not spin on its own axis, the sun is driven round by both the orbit and the rolling mesh, so with equal gears the shaft makes two turns per orbit.
explain.forces: The rod thrust acts at the mesh, tangential to the sun, so torque is the rod force times the pitch radius of the sun, varying with rod angle like a crank. The retaining link carries the radial separating force; the gear teeth and the link pivot are the weak points under shock.
explain.benefits: Gets rotary output from a reciprocating beam without a crank and doubles shaft speed compared with a crank. It has no dead centre in the way a single crank does at top and bottom.
explain.limits: More parts, gear wear and backlash than a simple crank, and the flywheel is still needed to smooth the torque. It fell out of use once the crank patent expired around 1794.

mechanisms.name: Worm drive
mechanisms.summary: A screw-like worm turns a toothed wheel on a crossing shaft, giving a large reduction in one stage that often cannot be driven backwards.

ratio.typical: 5:1 to 75:1 per stage (up to about 100:1); ratio = wheel teeth / worm starts; default 30:1

topology.notes: ground, worm, wheel; one worm mesh (screw-type sliding contact)

explain.motion: The worm is a screw with one thread (start). Each worm turn advances the wheel by one tooth, so a 30-tooth wheel turns once per 30 worm turns. The shafts cross at 90° without intersecting.
explain.forces: Contact is mostly sliding along the thread, so friction is high and efficiency falls from about 90% at low ratios to under 50% at high ratios. With a small lead angle (here 5.7°) friction exceeds the driving component when the wheel tries to turn the worm, so the drive locks.
explain.benefits: Very high reduction in one compact, quiet stage, and a self-locking worm holds loads without a brake in many uses.
explain.limits: Low efficiency and heat build-up; a steel worm needs a bronze wheel and good lubrication. Self-locking is unreliable under vibration, so it should not replace a safety brake on hoists.

mechanisms.name: Crossed helical gears
mechanisms.summary: Two helical gears on non-parallel, non-intersecting shafts touch at a point and drive each other, usually at 90°, for light loads.

ratio.typical: 1:1 to about 5:1; ratio = z2/z1 (not pitch diameter ratio); default 24/12 = 2:1

topology.notes: ground, gear 1, gear 2; one point-contact crossed helical mesh

explain.motion: Two ordinary helical gears of the same hand are mounted on shafts crossing at 90° at a set distance. With 45° helix angles the teeth line up and gear 1 (12 teeth) turns gear 2 (24 teeth) at half speed.
explain.forces: Contact is a single point that slides along the teeth, so load capacity is low and wear is high. Each gear sees an axial thrust that must be taken by its bearings.
explain.benefits: Lets two standard helical gears drive between skew shafts, and centre distance and ratio can be tuned by choosing different helix angles. Insensitive to small centre-distance errors.
explain.limits: Point contact and high sliding limit them to light power, such as camshaft-driven distributors and oil pumps; for real loads use a worm or hypoid set.

mechanisms.name: Cycloidal drive
mechanisms.summary: An eccentric drives a lobed disc around a ring of pins; one fewer lobe than pins gives a large, compact, shock-tolerant reduction.

ratio.typical: 10:1 to about 100:1 per stage; ratio = n / (N - n); default 11:1

topology.notes: ground with ring pins, eccentric input shaft, cycloidal disc, output flange with pins; higher pairs: disc lobes on ring pins (rolling), output pins in disc holes (pin-in-hole)

explain.motion: The input shaft carries an eccentric that makes the cycloidal disc wobble around inside a ring of 12 fixed pins. Because the disc has 11 lobes, one fewer than the pins, it rolls backwards by one lobe for every input turn, and pins on the output flange running in holes in the disc pick off that slow rotation.
explain.forces: Many lobes touch ring pins at once (in theory about half), so load is shared and the drive survives shock loads well. The eccentric disc creates an unbalanced force, so real units use two discs 180° apart.
explain.benefits: High ratio in one compact stage, rolling contact with high efficiency (often above 90%), high shock tolerance and low backlash.
explain.limits: Single discs vibrate unless balanced, the profile must be made precisely, and output torque has a small ripple. More parts than a planetary stage.

mechanisms.name: Differential
mechanisms.summary: Splits one input between two output shafts so they can turn at different speeds, their average always equal to the carrier speed.

ratio.typical: final drive 2.5:1 to 5:1 into the case; 1:1 average to the two side shafts; default 41/10 = 4.1:1

topology.notes: ground, input pinion, ring gear+case (carrier), left side gear, right side gear, spider pinions (2, counted as 1 body type); meshes: pinion-ring, 2 spiders x 2 side gears. Mobility 2: case speed and wheel speed difference

explain.motion: The input pinion turns the ring gear and the case it is bolted to. Spider pinions on a cross-pin in the case drive two side gears; when the car goes straight the spiders do not spin and both wheels turn with the case, and in a turn the spiders spin so the outer wheel speeds up as much as the inner slows down.
explain.forces: An open differential always gives equal torque to both outputs, so the wheel with least grip limits total traction. The spider pinions only carry load across their own teeth and turn only when the wheels differ in speed.
explain.benefits: Lets driven wheels on one axle cover different distances in a turn without scrubbing tyres, and as a mechanism it adds or averages two rotations exactly.
explain.limits: If one wheel loses grip it spins and the other gets almost no torque; limited-slip or locking differentials address this at the cost of complexity.

mechanisms.name: Harmonic drive
mechanisms.summary: An elliptical wave generator flexes a thin toothed cup inside a rigid ring with two more teeth, giving a 50:1 to 160:1 coaxial reduction with no backlash.

ratio.typical: 30:1 to 160:1 per stage; ratio = Zf / (Zc - Zf); default 100/2 = 50:1

topology.notes: ground with circular spline, wave generator, flexspline (compliant), plus the wave generator bearing rolling on the flexspline; one multi-tooth mesh at two zones

explain.motion: An elliptical cam with a thin ball bearing (the wave generator) spins inside a flexible cup with 100 external teeth (the flexspline), bending it so its teeth engage a rigid 102-tooth ring at the two ends of the long axis. Each wave generator turn shifts the flexspline back by two teeth relative to the ring, so the flexspline turns once, backwards, per 50 input turns.
explain.forces: About 30% of the teeth are in contact at once, giving high torque capacity and stiffness for the size. The flexspline is cyclically bent every half turn, so its fatigue strength sets the torque and life limits.
explain.benefits: High single-stage ratio, near-zero backlash, coaxial hollow-shaft design and light weight make it the standard robot joint reducer.
explain.limits: Torsional compliance is higher than in rigid gears, the flexspline can fail by fatigue or ratcheting under overload, and efficiency falls at high ratios and low temperatures.

mechanisms.name: Hypoid gear pair
mechanisms.summary: A spiral bevel pair with the pinion axis offset below the gear centre, so the shafts cross without meeting; used in car rear axles.

ratio.typical: 2.5:1 to 5:1 in car axles, up to about 10:1; default 41/10 = 4.1:1

topology.notes: ground, pinion, ring gear; one hypoid mesh with sliding along the tooth

explain.motion: The 10-tooth pinion drives a 41-tooth ring gear through 90°, but its axis passes 25 mm below the ring gear centre. To mesh at that offset the pinion has a larger spiral angle than the gear, which makes it larger and stronger than a spiral bevel pinion of the same ratio.
explain.forces: The offset adds sliding along the teeth, so tooth friction is higher than in a bevel pair and extreme-pressure hypoid oil is required. Contact is spread over several curved teeth at once, giving high load capacity and smooth, quiet running.
explain.benefits: The lowered pinion lets a car's propeller shaft sit lower (less floor tunnel), and the bigger pinion and higher contact ratio carry more torque quietly.
explain.limits: Efficiency (about 90 to 96%) is lower than bevel gears, requires special lubricant, and setup of pinion depth and backlash is critical. Manufacturing needs dedicated Gleason or Klingelnberg type machines.

mechanisms.name: Non-circular gears
mechanisms.summary: Gears with non-round pitch curves, such as a pair of ellipses turning on their foci, give a speed ratio that varies through each turn.

ratio.typical: ratio swings between (1-e)/(1+e) and (1+e)/(1-e) each turn; 0.54 to 1.86 at e = 0.3

topology.notes: ground, gear 1, gear 2; one non-circular gear mesh

explain.motion: Two identical elliptical gears each turn about one focus, with the foci 80 mm apart (the major axis length). As the driver turns steadily, the contact point moves along the ellipses, so the driven gear speeds up and slows down once per turn, from 0.54 to 1.86 times the input speed.
explain.forces: Torque transmitted scales inversely with the instantaneous speed ratio, so the driven shaft sees cyclic torque and the system sees inertia loads from the varying speed. Pressure angle varies along the profile, which limits the eccentricity before teeth jam or undercut.
explain.benefits: Produces an exact, repeatable non-uniform motion with continuous rotation, useful for quick-return strokes, matching cutter speed to web speed, or oval-gear flow metering.
explain.limits: Hard to design and manufacture (each tooth differs), noisier than round gears, and large eccentricity causes undercut and interference. Cams or linkages are often cheaper for one-off motion laws.

mechanisms.name: Planetary gear set
mechanisms.summary: Planets orbit a central sun inside a ring gear; hold the ring, drive the sun, and the carrier turns slowly in line with the input.

ratio.typical: 3:1 to 10:1 per stage with ring fixed; default 1 + 35/13 = 3.69:1

explain.motion: The sun drives three planets, which roll around inside the fixed ring and carry the carrier with them. With 13 sun teeth and a 35-tooth ring, the carrier turns once for every 1 + 35/13 = 3.69 turns of the sun, in the same direction, while each planet spins backwards on its own pin.
explain.forces: Load is shared between three planets, so each mesh carries about a third of the torque and the radial pushes on the sun cancel. The ring reacts the difference between input and output torque.
explain.benefits: Coaxial input and output, very high torque density, and by choosing which of sun, ring or carrier is held, the same parts give different ratios; with two inputs it adds or subtracts speeds.
explain.limits: Tooth counts are constrained by assembly and spacing rules, load sharing needs accurate parts or floating members, and the many meshes make it costlier than a simple pair.

mechanisms.summary: Two suns, short and long pinions on one carrier and a single ring give several forward ratios and reverse in a compact automatic gearbox.

mechanisms.name: Wankel rotary engine
mechanisms.summary: A triangular rotor orbits inside an epitrochoid housing, phased by a 3:2 internal gear, turning the eccentric shaft three times per rotor turn.

ratio.typical: eccentric shaft 3 turns per rotor turn (rotor gear : fixed gear = 3:2)

topology.notes: ground (housing with fixed external gear), eccentric shaft, rotor with internal gear; one gear mesh; apex seals sliding on the housing are redundant contacts

explain.motion: The rotor's internal gear rolls on a fixed gear on the housing, so the rotor centre orbits the shaft axis on the eccentric while the rotor turns slowly the same way. Its three apexes stay on the epitrochoid wall, forming three chambers that grow and shrink twice per rotor turn. The eccentric shaft turns three times for each rotor revolution, giving one power stroke per shaft turn per rotor.
explain.forces: Gas pressure on each rotor flank pushes through the rotor bearing onto the eccentric, producing torque equal to force times eccentricity. The phasing gears carry only the reaction that keeps the rotor in step, while apex seals take sliding contact loads and wear.
explain.benefits: Very compact and smooth for its power, with no reciprocating parts and few moving pieces.
explain.limits: Long thin combustion chambers burn poorly, giving higher fuel use and emissions. Apex seal wear and oil consumption limit life.

mechanisms.name: Star wheel and pin
mechanisms.summary: A finger on a turning shaft knocks a star wheel on by one tooth per turn, and a sprung jumper snaps it into place and holds it.

ratio.typical: 36° per driver turn (10 teeth); 31 teeth for a date wheel

topology.notes: ground, driver with finger pin, star wheel, jumper lever with roller; finger-star and jumper-star contacts; jumper spring

explain.motion: A driver turns continuously and once per turn its finger enters a gap of the star wheel and pushes one tooth. A spring-loaded jumper rides up the tooth flank and, once the tooth passes its peak, snaps the star forward into the next gap. Between pushes the jumper holds the star still.
explain.forces: The finger works against the jumper spring until the tooth tip passes, then the spring does the last part of the step. The finger load is light but the snap gives a small impact and holding force depends entirely on the spring.
explain.benefits: Very simple, cheap and compact, with a crisp, well-defined rest position. The output can step through any number of positions per revolution.
explain.limits: Holding is only spring force, so it suits light loads and slow rates. Backdriving with enough force can jump the jumper.

mechanisms.name: Geneva drive
mechanisms.summary: A pin on a constantly turning crank enters a slot and steps a slotted wheel a quarter turn, then a locking disc holds it still.

ratio.typical: 90° per index (4-slot), moving for 90° of crank, dwell 270°

topology.notes: ground, crank (arm with pin and locking disc), slotted wheel; pin-in-slot and locking arc contact alternate

explain.motion: The crank turns continuously; its pin enters a slot tangentially, drives the wheel through a quarter turn and leaves tangentially. While the pin is out, a raised locking disc on the crank sits in a concave arc on the wheel and holds it still. With 4 slots the wheel moves during 90° of crank rotation and rests for 270°.
explain.forces: The pin pushes on the slot wall; torque on the wheel is highest mid-index when the pin is closest to the wheel centre. Acceleration jumps at entry and exit, so impact and wear grow quickly with speed.
explain.benefits: Positive indexing and locking with very few parts, and the entry and exit have zero wheel velocity.
explain.limits: Infinite jerk at entry and exit limits speed, and the index angle is fixed by the slot count. The ratio of motion to dwell cannot be chosen freely.

mechanisms.name: Intermittent gear
mechanisms.summary: A gear with only a few teeth drives a full gear part of each turn; between bursts a locking rim holds the driven gear still.

ratio.typical: 90° per driver turn (5 of 20 teeth), dwell 270°

topology.notes: ground, mutilated driver with locking disc, driven gear with locking arcs; gear mesh and locking contact alternate

explain.motion: The driver has teeth on only part of its rim. While those teeth are in mesh, the driven gear turns at the normal gear ratio; when they pass, a plain locking disc on the driver rides in a concave arc on the driven gear and holds it still. Here 5 of 20 teeth advance the driven gear a quarter turn per driver turn.
explain.forces: During mesh it acts like an ordinary spur pair at a 20° pressure angle. The first tooth hits the driven gear at full pitch-line speed, so there is a shock at engagement that grows with speed.
explain.benefits: Any step size and dwell split can be set by tooth count, and the driven gear is positively located throughout.
explain.limits: Sudden start and stop cause impact, so it suits slow or light duty. Geneva or cam indexers are preferred at high speed or load.

mechanisms.name: Internal Geneva drive
mechanisms.summary: A crank pin works inside a cup-shaped slotted wheel, stepping it the same way as the crank with a longer, gentler move and shorter dwell.

ratio.typical: 90° per index (4-slot), moving for 270° of crank, dwell 90°

topology.notes: ground, crank with pin and locking cam, internal slotted wheel; pin-in-slot and locking contact alternate

explain.motion: The slotted wheel is a cup with slots pointing inward from its rim; the crank sits inside the cup with its axis offset from the wheel axis. The pin enters a slot tangentially and drives the wheel the same way as the crank for 270° of crank rotation, then a locking cam on the crank holds the wheel for the remaining 90°.
explain.forces: Since the move is spread over a longer crank angle, peak angular acceleration is much lower than in an external Geneva of the same slot count. The crank must be overhung (supported on one side only) because the wheel surrounds it.
explain.benefits: Smoother motion with lower peak acceleration, same-direction rotation and a compact package.
explain.limits: Dwell is short (less than half the cycle), and the overhung crank limits load. Hard to make with few slots because the pin path must fit inside the cup.

mechanisms.summary: A tapered rib cam on a constantly turning shaft steps a turret of rollers by one station, then locks it between the ribs.

ratio.typical: 45° per index (8 stops), index in 120° of camshaft, dwell 240°

topology.notes: ground, globoidal cam shaft, turret with radial rollers; two rollers in contact with the rib at all times (preloaded)

explain.motion: The input camshaft turns at constant speed. A raised rib wraps part way round a waisted (globoidal) cam; in its straight section it holds two turret rollers and the turret dwells, and in its twisted section it pushes the rollers along, rotating the turret one station. One cam turn gives one index.
explain.forces: Rollers are preloaded against both rib flanks, so there is no backlash and the turret is locked during dwell. Torque passes through rolling contact, and the cam law (modified sine) keeps peak acceleration and jerk low.
explain.benefits: High precision, high speed and no backlash, with smooth motion set by the cam law. Very rigid locking in dwell.
explain.limits: Expensive to make, fixed stop count and index time once cut, and needs a clutch or brake for overload. Bulky compared with a Geneva for light loads.

mechanisms.name: Barrel cam
mechanisms.summary: A helical groove around a rotating drum pushes a roller follower back and forth parallel to the drum axis.

ratio.typical: stroke = groove axial travel (40 mm by default) per drum turn

topology.notes: ground, drum, follower slide, roller; roller in groove is a form-closed cam contact

explain.motion: A groove cut around the drum surface wanders along the axis. A roller sitting in the groove is carried with it, so the follower slide moves parallel to the drum axis as the drum turns. The default groove rises over 160°, dwells 20°, returns over 160° and dwells 20°.
explain.forces: Groove walls push both ways, so no return spring is needed. The pressure angle is set by groove slope: tan(phi) = s'/Rp, where Rp is the pitch radius; a larger drum gives a gentler slope and lower side load.
explain.benefits: Positive (form-closed) motion along the shaft axis, compact for long strokes, and can hold several followers on one drum.
explain.limits: Groove backlash means the roller flips walls at reversals, causing wear and noise. Machining a 3D groove is costlier than a plate cam.

mechanisms.summary: A shaped disc lifts a roller follower along its guide, so the output motion is whatever profile you cut into the cam.

ratio.typical: stroke = rise h (22 mm by default) per cam turn

topology.notes: ground, cam, follower stem, roller; roller spin is a passive extra freedom; cam contact is the higher pair

explain.motion: As the cam turns, the roller rides its edge and the follower rises and falls along its guide. In this default the profile rises cycloidally over 180° and returns cycloidally over 180°; any timing, including long dwells, can be drawn into the outline.
explain.forces: The cam can only push along the contact normal through the roller centre. The pressure angle between that normal and the follower path decides how much of the push goes sideways into the guide; keep it under about 30°. A spring or gravity must hold the follower on the cam.
explain.benefits: Almost any motion law with two moving parts and exact timing. A roller turns sliding into rolling contact, cutting wear.
explain.limits: Needs a return spring, which can float at high speed. Large lift in a short angle forces a big cam or high pressure angles.

mechanisms.name: Cam with flat-faced follower
mechanisms.summary: A disc cam pushes a follower with a flat face, so contact slides across the face and the push always stays square to the stroke.

ratio.typical: stroke = rise h (15 mm by default) per cam turn

topology.notes: ground, cam, flat-faced follower; cam contact slides along the face

explain.motion: The cam turns and its lobe pushes the flat face of the follower up its guide. The contact point slides sideways across the face by a distance equal to ds/dtheta. The default profile rises cycloidally over 120°, dwells 60°, returns over 120° and dwells 60°.
explain.forces: The contact normal is always perpendicular to the face, so the pressure angle is zero for an in-line follower and guide side load comes only from friction and contact offset. The sliding contact carries high Hertz stress and needs good lubrication.
explain.benefits: Very compact and stiff with no side thrust from pressure angle, which suits direct-acting engine valves.
explain.limits: The cam must be convex everywhere (no concave flanks), and the face must be wide enough for the contact excursion. Sliding friction causes wear, so flat tappets need careful break-in.

mechanisms.name: Face groove cam
mechanisms.summary: A roller runs in a closed groove cut into the face of a disc, so the cam drives the follower both out and back without a spring.

ratio.typical: stroke = rise h (20 mm by default) per cam turn

topology.notes: ground, grooved disc, radial follower slide, roller; groove gives form-closed cam contact

explain.motion: The groove is a closed loop machined into the face of the disc; its distance from the centre varies with angle. The roller sits in the groove, so as the disc turns the follower is pulled in and pushed out along its radial guide. The default track rises over 120°, dwells 60°, returns over 120° and dwells 60° with a 3-4-5 polynomial law.
explain.forces: Either groove wall can push, so the follower is driven in both directions and cannot float. Pressure angle limits are the same as a plate cam; the roller reverses which wall it touches when acceleration changes sign.
explain.benefits: Positive motion with no return spring, so it works at high speed and in any orientation.
explain.limits: Roller wall-switching causes backlash, noise and wear, and the roller spins the wrong way when it touches the outer wall. A wider, heavier disc than a plate cam.

mechanisms.name: Desmodromic valve cam
mechanisms.summary: Two matched cams and rockers open and close a valve mechanically, so the valve follows the cam with no return spring.

ratio.typical: valve lift 10 mm per cam turn (camshaft at half crank speed)

topology.notes: ground, camshaft (opening and closing lobes), opening rocker, closing rocker, valve; cam-rocker and rocker-valve contacts; deliberately redundant (conjugate) constraint

explain.motion: An opening lobe pushes the opening rocker down onto the valve stem, opening the valve. A second, conjugate closing lobe drives a forked closing rocker that pulls up on a collar on the valve stem, closing it. The two profiles are cut so that at every angle one rocker or the other holds the valve, so lift follows the law exactly.
explain.forces: The opening cam carries gas and inertia loads on opening; the closing cam carries the inertia of deceleration and the closing pull that a spring would normally supply. Rocker sliding contacts carry high loads and need tight clearance control.
explain.benefits: No valve float at high revs and no spring force to overcome, so aggressive lift laws are possible.
explain.limits: Two clearances per valve to set, more parts and sliding friction, and conjugate profiles must be ground very accurately. Modern valve springs and pneumatic returns reduce its advantage.

mechanisms.name: Locomotive driving gear
mechanisms.summary: A piston, crosshead and main rod turn one driving wheel, and a coupling rod makes the next wheel turn exactly with it.

ratio.typical: stroke = 2 x crank radius (34 mm); coupled wheels turn 1:1

topology.notes: crosshead, main rod, two wheels, coupling rod, ground; the coupling loop is a parallelogram four-bar; count includes ground

explain.motion: Steam pushes the piston back and forth. The crosshead, sliding between guide bars, carries the piston rod and turns that push into the swinging main rod, which drives the crank pin on the main wheel. The coupling rod joins crank pins set at the same angle on both wheels, so it stays level, every point on it circles at crank radius, and the wheels turn together.
explain.forces: The crosshead takes the side thrust of the tilted main rod so the piston does not. Torque falls to zero at each dead centre, so real locomotives set the cranks on the two sides 90° apart (quartered) to always have one side able to start.
explain.benefits: Spreads tractive effort over several wheels for grip, with a simple, robust and inspectable rod drive.
explain.limits: Rods and counterweights cause hammer blow and shaking that pound the track. Each side alone has dead centres, and the parallelogram has change points where a slack rod could jam.
