mechanisms.name: Oldham coupling
mechanisms.summary: Two parallel offset shafts joined by a floating disc with crossed tongues; the output turns at exactly input speed while the disc centre circles twice per turn.

ratio.typical: exactly 1:1 at every instant; disc centre orbits at 2x shaft speed on a circle of diameter e

topology.notes: ground, input hub, floating disc (with both tongues), output hub; two prismatic tongue-in-slot pairs at right angles; a double-slider (elliptic trammel inversion)

explain.motion: Each shaft carries a hub with a straight slot across its face. The middle disc has two tongues at right angles, one on each face, and each tongue slides in one hub's slot. Because the tongues are square to each other, both hubs must turn through the same angle, and the disc's centre runs round a small circle between the two shaft centres, twice for every turn of the shafts.
explain.forces: Torque passes as side forces between the tongues and the walls of the slots, square to each slot. The offset itself puts little bending on the shafts, but the tongues slide back and forth once per turn, so the faces need lubrication or a low-friction disc and wear grows with offset and speed.
explain.benefits: The speed ratio is exactly one at every instant, unlike a single universal joint. It takes up parallel offset in a short length, and the middle disc can be a cheap plastic part that also insulates and acts as a torque fuse.
explain.limits: Only small offsets in practice (a few percent of diameter) because sliding wear and the orbiting disc's unbalance grow with offset. Little angular misalignment capacity and some backlash unless spring-loaded.

mechanisms.name: Universal joint
mechanisms.summary: Two yokes joined by a cross let shafts at an angle drive each other, but the output speed speeds up and slows down twice per turn.

ratio.typical: 1:1 on average; instantaneous ratio swings between cos(beta) and 1/cos(beta), 0.866 to 1.155 at 30°

topology.notes: ground, input yoke, cross (spider), output yoke; a spherical 4R chain with all four axes meeting at the cross centre

explain.motion: Each shaft ends in a fork (yoke), and the two forks are joined by a cross whose arms run in bearings in the forks. As the input turns, the cross wobbles so the output yoke follows round at an angle. Over a full turn both shafts turn 360°, but within the turn the output runs ahead and then behind, twice per revolution.
explain.forces: Torque passes through the cross arms as forces in the yoke bearings. The speed fluctuation causes angular acceleration of the output and its inertia, giving torque ripple and vibration that grows sharply with angle; the yokes also feel a secondary bending couple.
explain.benefits: Simple, strong and compact, it carries large torque across angles of up to about 30° to 45° and is cheap to make with needle-bearing crosses.
explain.limits: Not constant velocity: at 30° the output speed varies by about ±15%. Above about 45° it locks up, and it needs pairs (double cardan or phased driveshaft) to cancel the fluctuation.

mechanisms.name: Double Cardan joint
mechanisms.summary: Two universal joints back to back with a short centre yoke cancel each other's speed wobble, giving constant velocity across an angle.

ratio.typical: exactly 1:1 when both joint angles are equal and the centre yokes are in phase

topology.notes: ground, input yoke, cross 1, centre yoke, cross 2, output yoke; 2 shaft bearings plus 2 cross bearings per joint; a ball-and-socket centring device (spherical pair, not counted) keeps the two joint angles equal

explain.motion: The input yoke drives a first cross, which drives a short centre yoke, which drives a second cross and the output yoke. Each single joint makes the speed fluctuate, but because the two joints are set at equal angles with the centre yoke forks in the same plane, the second joint's speed-up exactly cancels the first one's slow-down. A centring ball and socket between the two shafts keeps the two angles equal as the total angle changes.
explain.forces: Torque passes through both crosses, each carrying it as yoke-bearing forces; the centre yoke still accelerates twice per turn, but the output does not. The centring device carries the small forces that keep the joint angles equal.
explain.benefits: Constant velocity at larger angles than a single U-joint can tolerate, using rugged, serviceable cross-and-bearing parts.
explain.limits: Longer, heavier and more complex than a single joint; constant velocity only holds when the two angles stay equal, and the centring ball wears.

mechanisms.name: Rzeppa CV joint
mechanisms.summary: Six balls held in a cage between grooved inner and outer races stay in the plane bisecting the shaft angle, so the output turns at constant speed.

ratio.typical: exactly 1:1 up to about 45° to 48° joint angle

topology.notes: ground, inner race with shaft, outer race (bell) with shaft, cage, 6 balls; each ball contacts an inner groove, an outer groove and a cage window (18 rolling/sliding higher pairs); cage to races are spherical sliding fits

explain.motion: The inner race on one shaft and the bell-shaped outer race on the other each have six curved grooves. Six balls sit in pairs of facing grooves and in windows of a cage that lies between the races. The groove shapes force the balls, and so the cage, to stay in the plane that bisects the angle between the shafts, which makes the joint symmetric and the two shafts turn at exactly the same speed.
explain.forces: Torque passes from inner race to balls to outer race as contact forces at the groove flanks; the cage only positions the balls. Load is shared between six balls, so it is compact for its torque, but contact stresses are high and need clean grease.
explain.benefits: True constant velocity at large angles in a compact package, ideal for steered driven wheels.
explain.limits: Needs a sealed boot full of grease; a torn boot lets in grit and it fails by clicking and wear. Fixed-type joints do not plunge, so a sliding (tripod or plunging) joint is needed at the other end of the shaft.

mechanisms.name: Schmidt coupling
mechanisms.summary: Three discs joined by sets of parallel links connect widely offset parallel shafts at exactly the same speed, with no side load.

ratio.typical: exactly 1:1 for any offset from near zero up to 2 x link length

topology.notes: ground, input disc, middle disc, output disc, 3 links between input and middle, 3 links between middle and output; 12 link-end pins plus 2 shaft bearings; overconstrained parallelogram sets (3 links where 2 would do, to pass dead centres)

explain.motion: The input disc is linked to a middle disc by three equal links whose pins sit on equal pitch circles 120° apart, and the middle disc is linked the same way to the output disc. Each set of links forms parallelograms, so the joined discs always keep the same orientation: all three discs turn at the same angle. The links themselves do not rotate; they only translate in circles, while the middle disc spins about a fixed point set by the offset.
explain.forces: Torque passes through the links in tension and compression, with the three links of each set sharing load so no set ever sits at a dead centre. Because the parallelograms leave no reaction at the shafts, there is no side load on the bearings from the offset.
explain.benefits: Exact constant velocity with large parallel offsets, and the offset can even change while running. Compact axially compared with a cardan shaft.
explain.limits: Many pins and bearings make it costlier and heavier than an Oldham or bellows coupling. Near zero offset the middle disc position becomes undetermined, so a small minimum offset or support is needed, and it takes little angular misalignment.

mechanisms.name: Lead screw
mechanisms.summary: A threaded shaft turning in a nut that is kept from rotating moves the nut along the shaft by one lead per turn, giving slow, strong linear motion.

ratio.typical: travel = lead per turn, e.g. 3 mm per turn (Tr12x3); leads from under 1 mm to 50 mm

topology.notes: ground, screw (revolute in end bearings), nut (prismatic on a guide); screw to nut is a helical (screw) pair, counted here as a lower pair outside revolute/prismatic

explain.motion: The screw turns in bearings at its ends while the nut is held by a guide so it cannot spin. Each turn of the screw slides the nut along the axis by one lead, the pitch times the number of starts. Reversing the screw reverses the nut.
explain.forces: The thread is an inclined plane wrapped round a cylinder, so a small torque gives a large axial thrust: ideal thrust F = 2 pi T / lead. Sliding friction on the flanks eats much of this, giving efficiencies of about 20% to 80%, and with small lead angles the friction angle exceeds the lead angle so the load cannot drive the screw back.
explain.benefits: Cheap, quiet, compact and holds its position without a brake when self-locking. Takes high loads and suits manual drives.
explain.limits: Low efficiency means heat and wear, so not for continuous high-speed duty. Backlash grows as the nut wears, and long slender screws whip at high speed (critical speed).

mechanisms.name: Ball screw
mechanisms.summary: A screw and nut with a stream of recirculating steel balls rolling between their grooves, turning rotation into precise, efficient linear motion.

ratio.typical: travel = lead per turn, commonly 5 to 12.7 mm per turn (16x5 default = 5 mm per turn)

topology.notes: ground, screw, nut; the ball train is a rolling higher pair acting as a screw pair; individual balls are not separate kinematic links for the model

explain.motion: Steel balls sit in matching helical grooves on the screw and inside the nut. As the screw turns, the balls roll along the groove and carry the nut axially by one lead per turn. At the end of the circuit a return tube, internal button or end cap lifts the balls out and feeds them back to the start, so they circulate endlessly.
explain.forces: Load passes through many rolling ball contacts instead of sliding flanks, so efficiency is around 90% and thrust is nearly 2 pi T / lead. Because it is so efficient, an axial load can spin the screw backwards, so vertical axes need a brake.
explain.benefits: High efficiency, long life, low heat and, with a preloaded double nut, zero backlash and high stiffness for precise positioning.
explain.limits: Not self-locking, more expensive than a lead screw, and sensitive to dirt and side load. Long screws are limited by critical speed and buckling.

mechanisms.name: Differential screw
mechanisms.summary: One shaft with two threads of slightly different pitch moves a nut by only the pitch difference per turn, giving very fine adjustment.

ratio.typical: travel = p1 - p2 per turn, e.g. 1.0 - 0.8 = 0.2 mm per turn

topology.notes: ground with fixed nut, screw with two threads, sliding nut on a guide; two screw (helical) pairs plus one prismatic guide

explain.motion: The screw carries two threads of the same hand but different pitch. One thread runs in a nut fixed to the frame, so each turn moves the screw itself forward by p1. The other thread carries a nut that is guided so it cannot turn; relative to the screw it moves back by p2, so its net motion is p1 - p2 per turn.
explain.forces: The effective lead is tiny, so the ideal force ratio is huge: F = 2 pi T / (p1 - p2). In practice friction in two thread pairs makes it strongly self-locking and fairly inefficient.
explain.benefits: Gives very fine motion with coarse, strong, easy-to-make threads instead of one very fine, fragile thread.
explain.limits: Low efficiency and slow travel, and backlash in two thread pairs adds up. Total stroke is limited by the length of the threads.

mechanisms.name: Belt drive
mechanisms.summary: A tensioned loop of belt wrapped round two pulleys carries rotation between distant shafts, changing speed by the ratio of pulley diameters.

ratio.typical: 1:1 to 6:1 per stage, ratio = D2/D1 (2:1 default)

topology.notes: ground, driving pulley, driven pulley, belt; two belt wraps as higher pairs; an idler/tensioner adds one revolute

explain.motion: Both pulleys are on parallel shafts and a tensioned belt runs round them. With no slip the belt speed is the same at each pulley rim, so the speeds are inversely proportional to the diameters. An open belt turns both pulleys the same way, a crossed belt reverses the output.
explain.forces: Torque is carried by the difference between the tight-side and slack-side tensions, limited by friction over the wrap angle (T1/T2 up to e^(mu theta)). Shaft bearings carry the sum of both tensions; small pulleys with short centre distance reduce wrap and grip.
explain.benefits: Quiet, cheap, tolerant of misalignment, spans long centre distances, needs no lubrication and slips on overload to protect the machine. Toothed timing belts add exact, slip-free timing.
explain.limits: Friction belts creep 0.5% to 1% and can slip, so the ratio is not exact. Belts stretch and age and need tension adjustment; not for very high torque in a small space.

mechanisms.name: Block and tackle
mechanisms.summary: A rope reeved through a fixed and a moving block of pulleys lifts a load with a pull divided by the number of rope parts holding it.

ratio.typical: MA = number of supporting rope parts, 2:1 (gun tackle) to 6:1 (threefold purchase); 4:1 default

topology.notes: ground with fixed block, moving block (vertical guide idealised as prismatic), 4 sheaves on their pins; rope wraps on each sheave as higher pairs; rope is a flexible member

explain.motion: The rope is tied to one block and threaded alternately round the sheaves of the fixed upper block and the moving lower block. Pulling the free end (the fall) shortens every rope part between the blocks equally, so the load rises by the pull distance divided by the number of supporting parts.
explain.forces: Each supporting part carries the same tension, so the hauling force is the load divided by n in the ideal case. Sheave bearing and rope bending friction add a few percent per sheave, so real advantage is lower and too many sheaves can cancel the gain.
explain.benefits: Very simple, light and portable, uses ordinary rope, and the advantage is easy to change by re-reeving.
explain.limits: Long hauling distance for a small lift, friction losses and twisting of the rope. Not self-locking: the load runs back if the fall is released, so a cleat or brake is needed.

mechanisms.name: Chain drive
mechanisms.summary: A roller chain meshing with toothed sprockets carries rotation between parallel shafts with no slip, in the ratio of tooth counts.

ratio.typical: 1:1 to 7:1 per stage, ratio = z2/z1 (30/15 = 2:1 default)

topology.notes: ground, driving sprocket, driven sprocket, chain (treated as one flexible member); two sprocket-chain meshes as higher pairs; each chain link is internally a revolute chain

explain.motion: The chain is a loop of pin-jointed links whose rollers sit between sprocket teeth. As the driver turns, each tooth pulls a roller, the tight span drags the driven sprocket round, and the slack span returns. Speeds are inversely proportional to tooth counts because the same number of links pass each sprocket.
explain.forces: Torque is carried only by the tight span tension; the slack span hangs nearly unloaded. Because the chain wraps as a polygon, the effective radius rises and falls once per tooth (chordal action), causing small speed ripple and impact as each roller seats, worst on small sprockets.
explain.benefits: No slip, high load in a compact width, efficiency up to about 98%, and long centre distances with simple parts. Several shafts can be driven from one chain.
explain.limits: Needs lubrication and protection from dirt, wears and stretches, and is noisier than a belt. Chordal speed variation and vibration limit high-speed use with small sprockets.

mechanisms.name: Belt CVT (variable pulley)
mechanisms.summary: Two V-pulleys with movable cone halves change their working diameters together, so a belt gives a stepless ratio.

ratio.typical: about 0.4:1 to 2.5:1 here (spread about 6.2); car CVTs typically spread 5 to 7

topology.notes: ground, input shaft with fixed sheave, input movable sheave, output shaft with fixed sheave, output movable sheave, belt; movable sheaves slide on splines; ratio setting is a second, controlled freedom

explain.motion: Each pulley is a pair of cones; one cone can slide along the shaft. Squeezing the input cones together pushes the belt outward to a larger radius, while the output cones spread so the belt sinks inward, which raises the output speed. Because the belt length is fixed, the two radii change together and the ratio moves smoothly between the limits.
explain.forces: Torque is carried by friction between the belt flanks and the sheave cones, so large clamping forces, from springs, flyweights or hydraulics, are needed. A steel push belt transmits by compression between its elements; rubber belts by tension.
explain.benefits: Keeps the engine at its best speed with no shift steps, simple to automate, and smooth.
explain.limits: Torque is limited by clamping force and belt strength, efficiency is a few percent below gears, and belts wear or slip if overloaded.

mechanisms.name: Friction wheel drive
mechanisms.summary: A rubber-rimmed wheel pressed on the face of a spinning disc turns faster the farther out it sits, giving a stepless, reversible ratio.

ratio.typical: omega_w / omega_d = R / r_w, 0.5 to 3.0 here; through zero to reverse

topology.notes: ground, disc, wheel on a splined shaft; the wheel's position along its shaft is a ratio setting (extra slide not counted)

explain.motion: The engine turns a flat disc. A wheel with a rubber or fibre rim presses on the disc face and can slide along its own shaft, which runs across the disc. Near the centre the wheel turns slowly, far out it turns fast, and moving it past the centre reverses it.
explain.forces: Torque transmitted is limited to mu x normal force x contact radius on the disc side. A spring or lever keeps the wheel pressed on; the high normal force loads both bearings. Different parts of the contact patch move at different speeds, causing scrubbing, heat and rim wear.

mechanisms.name: Ball-and-disc integrator
mechanisms.summary: A ball set at an adjustable radius on a turning disc drives an output roller, so the output angle is the integral of the radius.

ratio.typical: omega_out = omega_disc x x / r_c, reversing through zero at the disc centre

topology.notes: ground, disc, carriage, ball, output cylinder; ball rolls on disc and cylinder and is held in the carriage cage

explain.motion: A flat disc turns with the input variable, say time. A ball pressed onto its face is held by a carriage at distance x from the disc centre, and the ball also touches a cylinder whose axis is parallel to the carriage travel. The ball turns at a speed proportional to x, so the cylinder angle accumulates the integral of x over the disc angle, and moving the ball past the centre reverses it.
explain.forces: Only a small torque can be passed by rolling friction, so the output must be very lightly loaded or followed by a torque amplifier. Sliding across the contact when the carriage moves causes slight error and wear.
explain.benefits: Solves integration continuously and exactly in principle with simple parts, and allows smooth reversal through zero.
explain.limits: Very low output torque, slip errors under load, and accuracy depends on flat, clean, hard surfaces.

mechanisms.name: Anchor escapement
mechanisms.summary: An anchor-shaped pallet rocked by a pendulum lets the clock's escape wheel advance one tooth every two swings, metering out the train's power.

ratio.typical: 1 tooth (12°) per full pendulum period on a 30-tooth wheel, 6° per beat; wheel turns once a minute with a seconds pendulum

topology.notes: ground, escape wheel, anchor with pendulum rigidly attached; one intermittent cam-type contact between a wheel tooth and one of the two pallet faces

explain.motion: The weight or spring turns the escape wheel, but one of the two pallets of the anchor always blocks a tooth. As the pendulum swings, the anchor rocks on its arbor and lifts one pallet clear; the wheel jumps forward until a tooth drops onto the other pallet. Each swing releases half a tooth, so the wheel advances one tooth per full pendulum period. In the recoil form the wheel is pushed back slightly as the pendulum completes its swing.
explain.forces: The wheel tooth slides along the sloped pallet face and gives the pendulum a small push (impulse) each beat to make up for friction losses. The pendulum's own period, set by its length, governs the rate; the recoil couples train force into the pendulum, so rate varies with drive force.
explain.benefits: Only needs a small pendulum arc of about 4° to 6°, so long pendulums keep near-isochronous time. Simple, robust and cheap to make.
explain.limits: Recoil interferes with the pendulum and causes wear at the pallets, so accuracy is lower than the deadbeat form. Needs oiling at the pallet faces and is sensitive to clock being out of beat.

mechanisms.name: Verge escapement
mechanisms.summary: A crown wheel's teeth push alternately on two flag pallets on a vertical verge, rocking a foliot bar to and fro and letting the wheel creep round.

ratio.typical: one tooth per full foliot swing (24° on a 15-tooth crown wheel); foliot swings 80° to 100°

topology.notes: ground, crown wheel, verge with pallets and foliot; one intermittent cam-type contact between a crown tooth and the upper or lower pallet

explain.motion: The crown wheel has saw teeth on its rim, pointing along its axis, and odd tooth count. The verge is a rod across the wheel face carrying two flag pallets set about 90° to 105° apart, one engaging the top of the wheel and one the bottom. A tooth pushes one pallet round until it slips off, by which time the opposite pallet has swung into the path of a tooth on the far side, which stops and then reverses the verge. The foliot, a bar with weights, rocks back and forth with each push.
explain.forces: The wheel is in contact with a pallet nearly all the time, so drive torque directly sets the swing speed: there is no free natural period in the foliot form. Recoil happens every beat as the foliot's inertia drives the wheel backwards.
explain.benefits: Very simple and tolerant of crude workmanship, the first all-mechanical escapement. Works with a foliot, balance wheel or wide-swinging pendulum.
explain.limits: Rate depends strongly on drive force and friction, so early clocks drifted by up to an hour or more a day. Large swing and constant recoil cause wear.

mechanisms.name: Lever escapement
mechanisms.summary: A pallet lever between escape wheel and balance wheel unlocks the train and kicks the balance once per swing, leaving it free the rest of the time.

ratio.typical: half a tooth (12°) per beat on a 15-tooth wheel; 18,000 to 36,000 beats per hour

topology.notes: ground, escape wheel, pallet lever (fork), balance with roller and impulse pin; higher pairs are wheel tooth on pallet stone and impulse pin in the fork slot; banking pins are stops on ground

explain.motion: The balance wheel swings freely under its hairspring. Near the middle of each swing the impulse pin on the balance roller enters the lever fork and flicks the lever over, which lifts one pallet stone and lets an escape wheel tooth slide across the stone's impulse face. The tooth pushes the lever, the fork pushes the pin, and the balance gets its impulse; then the other pallet locks the next tooth and the lever rests against a banking pin while the balance completes its free arc.
explain.forces: Train torque reaches the balance only during the short impulse; the rest of the swing is detached. Draw, the angled locking faces, pulls the lever against its banking so shocks do not unlock it. Friction at the pallet stones needs oil and is the main loss.
explain.benefits: The balance is free for most of its swing, so timekeeping is good and robust to position and shock. It is the standard escapement of almost all mechanical watches.
explain.limits: Sliding friction at the pallets needs lubrication and wears; oil ageing changes the rate. Small, precise parts make it expensive to make and adjust.

mechanisms.name: Ratchet and pawl
mechanisms.summary: A rocking lever's pawl pushes a toothed wheel forward one tooth per stroke while a second pawl stops it slipping back.

topology.notes: ground, lever, ratchet wheel, driving pawl, holding pawl; pawl tips contact wheel teeth; springs keep pawls engaged (pawl angles follow the wheel)

explain.motion: The lever swings back and forth about the wheel axis. On the forward stroke its driving pawl catches the steep face of a tooth and pushes the wheel one tooth; on the return stroke it rides up over the sloped backs of the teeth. A holding pawl on the frame drops into each tooth to stop the wheel running back.
explain.forces: Load passes through the pawl tip on the steep tooth face; the face is undercut slightly so the pawl is pulled into engagement under load. The small backward movement before the holding pawl catches is the backlash, at most one tooth pitch.
explain.benefits: Simple, robust one-way drive and lock that can hold heavy loads.
explain.limits: Noisy, motion is in discrete steps, and backlash up to one pitch. Shock loads at engagement wear tooth faces and pawl tips.

mechanisms.name: Sprag clutch
mechanisms.summary: Tilted figure-eight sprags between two races slip one way and wedge the other, so torque passes in one direction only.

ratio.typical: 1:1 when locked; free when the outer race overruns

topology.notes: ground, inner race, outer race, one sprag (in practice 12 to 30 sprags in a cage with a garter spring); two friction contacts per sprag

explain.motion: Each sprag is a short strut slightly longer than the gap between the races, tilted by a light spring. When the inner race tries to turn faster than the outer in the driving direction, friction tips the sprags upright so they wedge and lock the races together. In the other direction the sprags lean over and slide, letting the outer race overrun freely.
explain.forces: Torque goes through many sprags in compression across the gap, so capacity is high for the size. Locking depends on the gripping angle staying below the friction angle (typically 3° to 5° against a friction coefficient around 0.1).
explain.benefits: Engages almost instantly with very little backlash and runs silently when overrunning, unlike a pawl ratchet.
explain.limits: Relies on friction and race hardness; wrong lubricant or worn races can let it slip or roll over. Drag and wear when overrunning at high speed.

mechanisms.name: Sarrus linkage
mechanisms.summary: Two hinged limbs set at right angles join a base and a top plate, so the top plate can only move straight up and down with no slide.

ratio.typical: plate height h = 2L cos(theta), up to 2L

topology.notes: base, top plate and two limbs of two links each; overconstrained, the Grubler count gives 0 but the two limbs share the one vertical freedom

explain.motion: Each limb is two equal links hinged to the base, to each other at a knee, and to the top plate, with all three hinge axes of a limb parallel. One limb alone lets the top plate move in one vertical plane; the second limb, turned 90 degrees, only allows motion in a plane at right angles. The only motion both allow is straight up and down, so the top plate rises along an exact line as the knees fold.
explain.forces: A vertical load on the plate becomes compression or tension in the limb links and a bending moment at the knees; near full extension the links are almost straight and carry large loads with little torque. Side loads and twisting are resisted by the hinges of the crossed limb, so hinge play shows up as wobble.
explain.benefits: An exact straight line with only revolute hinges, no guide rails, and the plates stay parallel with no rotation.
explain.limits: Travel is limited to less than twice the link length and the hinges must be stiff and accurate because the linkage is overconstrained. At full extension the knees reach a singular, straight position from which it cannot be driven back by a vertical push alone.

mechanisms.name: Swash plate
mechanisms.summary: A tilted disc on a shaft pushes a ring of pistons parallel to the shaft in and out once per turn, as in axial piston pumps.

ratio.typical: stroke = 2 R tan(gamma), 21.4 mm for R = 40, gamma = 15°

topology.notes: ground (cylinder block), shaft with swash plate, 5 pistons; each piston shoe slides on the plate face (higher pair)

explain.motion: A disc set at an angle gamma to the shaft rotates with it. Pistons arranged in a circle parallel to the shaft press against the disc face through slippers, so each piston moves in and out once per turn with simple harmonic motion, the pistons phased evenly round the circle. Changing gamma changes the stroke, and at zero angle the pistons stop.
explain.forces: Piston pressure force acts normal to the plate face, splitting into an axial thrust on the shaft bearing and a tangential part that makes the driving or driven torque. Shoe friction and the side load on pistons grow with the swash angle, which is why angles are kept below about 18°.
explain.benefits: Very compact, many pistons share one shaft for smooth flow, and the angle can be varied for displacement control.
explain.limits: Slipper and piston side loads limit the swash angle, and high-pressure contact faces need hydrostatic lubrication and clean fluid.

mechanisms.name: Bennett linkage
mechanisms.summary: A four-bar loop with skew hinge axes that still moves with one degree of freedom, thanks to a special balance of lengths and twists.

ratio.typical: tan(th1/2) tan(th2/2) = sin((b + a)/2) / sin((b - a)/2) for twists a, b

topology.notes: spatial 4R, overconstrained: Kutzbach gives -2 but the special geometry gives 1

explain.motion: Four links are joined in a loop by four hinges whose axes are skew, not parallel. Opposite links are equal in length and twist, and the lengths and twists obey a/sin(alpha) = b/sin(beta). With that balance the loop closes in a continuous family of positions, so turning one hinge drives the others, and the whole loop folds and unfolds in space.
explain.forces: Because the mobility depends on exact geometry, loads are shared redundantly across the joints and small errors in length or twist cause binding and internal stress. Torque between adjacent links varies strongly with position.
explain.benefits: The only movable spatial four-bar with revolute joints, very few parts, and it can fold flat in some configurations for deployable structures.
explain.limits: Very sensitive to manufacturing errors and joint play, and its spatial motion is hard to use for ordinary machine tasks.

mechanisms.name: Flexure hinge
mechanisms.summary: A thin, bendable section of one solid part acts as a pivot, giving smooth, friction-free rotation over a small angle.

ratio.typical: rotation stiffness K = 2 E b t^2.5 / (9 pi R^0.5), about 13 N·m/rad here

topology.notes: one compliant joint modelled as a revolute with a torsional spring (pseudo-rigid-body model); in reality a single monolithic part

explain.motion: A circular notch cut from both sides of a solid bar leaves a thin neck. Applying a moment bends the neck, so the part beyond it rotates almost about the neck centre, as if pinned. The rotation is limited to a few degrees in metal, or much more in a polypropylene living hinge.
explain.forces: The hinge behaves like a torsional spring of stiffness K, so the driver must supply both the load torque and K times the angle. Bending stress peaks at the thinnest section and limits the safe angle; the neck is weak against off-axis loads and buckling.
explain.benefits: No friction, no backlash and no wear, no lubrication, and precise repeatable motion that can be cut in one piece by wire EDM or moulding.
explain.limits: Small range of motion, fatigue at the neck if overstressed, and the centre of rotation shifts slightly with load and angle.

mechanisms.name: Bistable compliant mechanism
mechanisms.summary: Flexible inclined beams hold a shuttle in either of two stable positions and snap it through the middle when pushed.

ratio.typical: two stable positions at ±L0 sin(theta0) = ±6.9 mm; snap-through at the centre

topology.notes: pseudo-rigid-body model: ground, shuttle, and two beams each split into two telescoping parts with an axial spring; flex ends as pins; shuttle on a guide. Real part is one piece

explain.motion: Two flexible beams angled from fixed anchors meet at a central shuttle. Pushing the shuttle toward the centre line compresses the beams, which store energy until the shuttle passes the middle, after which the beams push it on into the mirror-image stable position. It stays there with no power until pushed back.
explain.forces: Force rises from zero at a stable position to a peak, falls through zero at the unstable centre and becomes negative, so the shuttle snaps. The beams carry mostly axial compression, and peak strain occurs near the anchors and shuttle.
explain.benefits: Holds two positions with zero power, one-piece construction with no wear, and gives a crisp tactile switching action.
explain.limits: The snap can be violent and the switching force depends strongly on material and tolerance; plastic beams creep, lowering force over time.
